1:
The form is a funeral song, and the voices say so before anything else. Clarke calls this the second part of the prophecy against Tyre, conducted in the manner of the old laments in which hired mourners first recited whatever was great in the dead and only then wept for the fall; on that plan the riches fill most of the chapter, the ruin is dispatched in a single allegorical verse of astonishing brevity, and the maritime world is left alarmed for itself. Gill describes the same convention, an elegy sung to say all that could be said in praise of the dead. Henry adds why one is called for here. Tyre stood at the height of its prosperity with no symptom of decay, and that prosperity was the snare, feeding a pride that would make the fall worse; those who live at ease are to be lamented if they are not preparing for trouble.

Henry then states a principle that Wesley repeats almost word for word: we ought to mourn for the miseries of other nations as well as our own, out of an affection for mankind in general, even where a people have brought the trouble on themselves. Henry alone adds the ground, that bewailing their calamities is part of the honour owed to all men.

The site is described with unusual precision. Gill puts the city at the eastern end of the great sea, half a mile off the mainland and well placed for shipping; Clarke calls it a small island, or rather a rock, and notes that a second Tyre stood on the shore, the two reckoned one city. Wesley gives the distance as four furlongs, the city lying as it were in the very door of the sea. Ellicott presses the wording: the term rendered entry is plural and means approaches or harbours, of which Tyre had two, both excellent — one facing south, the other north with an outer roadstead formed by a ledge off the island's north-west point — the first now wholly and the second nearly choked with sand and ruins. Gill notes that the borders in the midst of the seas stood so until a Macedonian siege turned the island into a peninsula.

The boast is where Henry fastens. To claim perfect beauty is to claim universal beauty, accomplishment on every side and admiration everywhere; and he sets against it the older title given to Zion, called the perfection of beauty because it had the beauty of holiness, whereas this city, well built and full of money and trade, sets up for the same on other grounds. It is the folly of the children of this world, he says, to reckon themselves beautiful because they are wealthy, and to think themselves perfect wherever they excel; nobody should count himself beautified further than he is sanctified, or claim perfect beauty on this side of heaven. Keil and Delitzsch render the verses plainly: the city dwelling at the approaches of the sea, merchant of the nations to many islands, its territory in the heart of the seas, its beauty perfected by its builders.

From here the city becomes a ship. Clarke identifies the allegory at once and sets beside it a Latin ode in which a commonwealth is drawn the same way, a vessel with stripped decks, a wounded mast, groaning yards and torn sails, warned to make for harbour and reminded that a painted stern is no comfort in a storm; he offers it as a parallel to many passages in the chapter. Henry explains why the praise comes first: elegies conventionally insert encomiums of those whose fall is lamented, so the prophet says what can be said. What he does not say is as pointed — nothing of Tyre's religion, her piety, or her charity to neighbours in distress.
5:
The ship is built out of a gazetteer. Gill and Clarke agree that Senir is the mountain the Sidonians called Sirion, and Gill takes the dual form of the word for planking as the two sides of the hull. Ellicott confirms the dual and adds a reason for the unfamiliar name: the prophet wanted a foreign one, and the alternative may by then have fallen out of use. On the tree he is candid: the Scripture names of trees are not always well identified, and what is called fir here is the timber supplied for the temple floor, which may have been spruce or cypress — both prized for shipbuilding, the cypress especially for lightness and freedom from worm.

The next verse is harder than it looks. Gill notes that the oaks of Bashan supplied only the oars, though the country was famous for oaks and one might have expected hulls; the ships, he supposes, were galleys. Clarke reports that some render the wood alder and others pine, and takes the disputed second term for boxwood. Ellicott sets out the difficulty exactly. Two words are of doubtful meaning, so the clause reads literally that they made thy something of tooth, daughter of something; the first is used elsewhere of the tabernacle boards and must mean planking, but it is singular and cannot well be benches, since a galley carried two or three tiers of those a side, and is now generally taken of the decking; and if the two Hebrew words presently written apart are joined, the second yields in box-wood. Wesley has box shipped from the Aegean and inlaid with ivory by Tyrian craftsmen.

Linen sails strike Ellicott as needing defence, since to a modern sailor the material would seem extravagant and too weak; but the state ships of antiquity were often rigged so, the embroidery serving instead of a pennon. Clarke thinks the flag rather than the sail is meant. On the purple, Ellicott places Elishah on the coasts of Asia Minor, where the shellfish were taken when the Tyrian coast could not supply the dye-works; Clarke puts Elishah in the Peloponnese, Wesley in Aeolis among people skilled at dyeing wool, calling the covering what a boatman would call a tilt.

Then the crew, and the division of labour is the point. Ellicott has the Phoenician towns furnish the oarsmen while Tyre supplied the captains and pilots; Wesley puts it less delicately, that the rich Tyrians would not employ their own in servile work and hired strangers, keeping their learned men for navigation, which was their great study. Gill reports what travellers of his own day found on the island that sent the rowers: a magnificent prospect from the mainland that resolves on arrival into one weak castle with a few small guns. Clarke explains what caulking is, hemp and pitch driven into the seams, and Ellicott identifies the town that supplied the workmen, reading the whole list as showing the dispersed Phoenician race tributary to the works of Tyre.

With the soldiers the figure of the ship is dropped, as Ellicott notes, so the military strength can be stated plainly. Keil and Delitzsch describe hired troops protecting the colonies while Phoenicians manned the walls, identify two of the three peoples as African rather than Asiatic, and find the mention of Persia surprising; Ellicott agrees on the descent and suggests the Persian soldiers came through the trade of the Gulf. Clarke's comment is drier: skilful and desperate men will go anywhere after their price. The last name defeats everyone. Clarke lists a Phoenician people, guardian images and simply strong men, and dismisses the old rendering that made them pygmies a cubit high. Wesley guesses a town called Gammade; Ellicott denies that any such people is known, thinks it unlikely that watch-towers would be manned by foreigners, and would translate the word brave men.
12:
The catalogue that follows is a customs ledger, and Clarke says so: the places and their imports are entered as regularly as in a European custom-house. Ellicott explains the recurring term the translators rendered fairs. It occurs only in this chapter, is rendered wares at its last appearance, and should be so throughout, the idea being something left with one party in place of something given in exchange, barter being what ancient commerce chiefly was. He reads the section as a survey of the nations not already named, and notes that the prophet varies his synonyms to avoid monotony.

Tarshish opens the list, its location unsettled. Clarke canvasses the Carthaginians, a port near the western straits, and a town in Cilicia, noting that the place was famous for silver, iron, tin and lead, all of which might have come from Britain. Ellicott settles on the Spanish site and agrees about the metals. Gill records the reading that takes the name simply for the sea.

The next entry is a slave market, and Clarke will not let it pass: these peoples trafficked in slaves, and the bodies and souls of men were bought and sold then as in his own degenerate age. Ellicott identifies the two northern names with tribes between the Black and Caspian seas, famous for slaves and for the copper their mountains still hold. Wesley notes only that they brought men to sell.

One entry defeats the received text. Ellicott points out that this is the single place in the enumeration where a name appears with a conjunction attached, and that there is no sense in finding here a tribe of Israel long since deported, the town of that name being too obscure for such a list; so what was taken for the conjunction is probably part of a name, an Arabian place some identify with Aden. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by the same route, calling it decisive that no other land or people in the list is introduced with that particle, and add that the second name here is not Greece but an Arabian district. Ellicott would also read the words rendered going to and fro as a town, the region's ancient capital; Clarke keeps both names Greek and takes the disputed phrase for importing and exporting, while allowing it may be a proper name.

Two places share a name and are not the same. Ellicott separates a Hamite tribe on the Persian Gulf from a Semitic one named later, and takes the many isles of the first for the Gulf islands that fed the Tyrian trade; he glosses horns of ivory as horns of teeth, horn being a merchant's term from the shape of a tusk, and notes that the word for ebony occurs only here, the Ethiopian wood preferred to the Indian. Where the list turns to Israel the difficulty is different: Ellicott places the wheat country in Ammon but confesses the next word unknown, and that it may not be a place name at all but some sweet confection such as grape syrup. Wesley calls it an obscure place now forgotten; Clarke suspects the clause names goods rather than towns.

Two corrections close the section. Ellicott would replace chests of rich apparel with treasures of twisted yarn, and strong for made of cedar, since a large trade in yarn ran from Babylonia to Tyre to be dyed and woven there. On the last verse he notes that ships of Tarshish means vessels of the largest class, as one might now say an East Indiaman, and that the word the translators took for singers is uncertain, opinion dividing between bulwarks and caravans — either yielding good sense, that the great ships were at once the city's defence and the means of its trade, or that they were its caravans of the sea. He prefers the first.
26:
The wreck comes in a single verse, and the voices agree who steered into it. Gill and Wesley make the rowers the rulers and counsellors, and the great waters the straits they brought on themselves by provoking Babylon; Wesley reads the east wind as that king with his army, the past tense as certainty, and notes the sting in the place of it, broken where she thought herself impregnable. Clarke has the trading vessels of every nation towing her into deep water, which is to say into affluence, before the storm dashes her to pieces. Ellicott resumes the figure soberly: oars were the main means of moving a ship before sailing was well understood, and the east wind in that sea is genuinely dangerous.

Henry draws the moral without softening it. The most magnificent states have their day to come down, and begin to decline at the zenith; but this ruin was sudden, the sun going down at noon, and the wealth that made the city great made the fall more grievous. The ship was split by the indiscretion of her own steersmen, who involved her in a war by mismanagement and then, holding out obstinately, enraged the enemy into destroying the state altogether. It goes ill with a people, he says, when those at the stern do not steer them into safety.

What follows is a list of everything that sinks at once. Keil and Delitzsch render it out — the riches and the sales, the bartering wares, seamen and sailors, the men who repaired the leaks and the men who trod the wares, the fighting men and all the multitude — and Ellicott presses the word governing it, which should be read with rather than in, so that every class making up the city's strength goes down with the ship. Clarke puts it flatly: laden with valuables and manned as well as a ship could be, she struck, and all of it went to the bottom. Gill notes that what was years in gathering was lost in a day.

Then the noise. Ellicott observes that the word rendered suburbs means the open ground about a place, and since Tyre had no land around her it must mean her surroundings generally; Gill has the cry carrying to the mainland and the towns belonging to her, and Wesley thinks the shore nearest the sea heard it first. Clarke abandons commentary at this point and testifies. He has heard the cry raised when a ship is driven on rocks with the helm useless, and says nothing more dismal can be imagined, the shout when all is lost being worse than the cry of fire at midnight; he asks the reader whether he has ever been wrecked on a lee shore, and says plainly that he describes a scene he witnessed himself, among the wretched.

The mourners are the smaller craft. Ellicott keeps the allegory running: the colonies and dependencies escape to shore and lament their mistress, and the preposition should be over rather than against, these trading nations being not hostile but wailing for her across the sea that swallowed her. Keil and Delitzsch note that the consternation is such that sailors abandon their own ships as no longer safe, and that the prophet heaps up every customary act of grief — dust, ashes, the shaved head, sackcloth, bitter weeping and a dirge. On the last word the voices divide. Clarke takes the hissing for a shriek, the sound spectators make as a vessel goes under. Ellicott denies that it is derision or terror and gives the verb its sense of calling for: those who traded with her will call and she will not answer, being not a terror but a sudden end, and not for ever. Gill keeps the plainer sense of scorn, recalling that Tyre had done the same over Jerusalem in hope of inheriting her trade.
